transcript: Dead Outlaw is now on Broadway and I'm pleased to report that it's just as strange as it was when it premiered downtown last year. Following the true story of Elmer McCurdy before and after his death, this is a darkly comedic tale on the meaning and meaninglessness of life paired with a folky-rock-country-grassroots score. As I mentioned, this is a strange musical, and it gets even stranger as it goes along, but that's part of its charm. It's pretty unorthodox in its storytelling. Aside from Andrew Durand who is wonderful in the leading role of Elmer, the rest of the ensemble assumes other characters as they come in and out for one-off plot points. With this, you don't really get to invest in specific characters and their development, but the overarching story is pretty wild and told in a very engaging way, as if you're gathered around a campfire for story time. I think it's best to not know what happens and to just let it surprise you. For me, since I saw it off-Broadway as well, it didn't hit quite the same the second time around, as the novelty of the plot itself wasn't there anymore. I also think it didn't hit quite the same in a larger venue, though the music is still wonderful, and I hope the score gets some recognition come award season. In any case, I am glad it's getting the Broadway treatment so more people can experience it, and I love how the irony alluded to in the show of how Elmer McCurdy's existence is more eventful after his death is furthered by the fact that now there's a Broadway musical about him. If you're down for something different, Dead Outlaw is in previews at the Longacre Theatre. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
